title: Cluster networking
summary: The flat pod network, CNI, how a ClusterIP is really implemented, CoreDNS, Ingress and NetworkPolicy.

concepts.title: The flat pod network and CNI
concepts.brief:
Kubernetes assumes one thing about networking: **every pod can reach every other pod by IP, without NAT**. It does not implement that — a **CNI plugin** does.

How it usually works: each node gets a slice of the cluster CIDR (`podCIDR`, typically a /24), the CNI hands out IPs from that slice, and node-to-node traffic is either routed directly (Calico BGP or a routed underlay) or encapsulated in VXLAN (Flannel/Canal).

RKE2 ships **Canal** by default (Flannel for the dataplane + Calico for NetworkPolicy), with Calico and Cilium as supported alternatives.

Things that follow from the model:

- Pod IPs are ephemeral — they change on every restart, which is why Services exist
- All containers in a pod share one network namespace, so they talk over `localhost` and cannot both bind the same port
- VXLAN adds ~50 bytes of overhead; if the underlay MTU is 1500 the pod MTU must drop to ~1450 or you get the classic 'small requests work, large ones hang' bug

examples.label: Per-node pod CIDRs
examples.code:
$ kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CIDR:.spec.podCIDR
NAME    CIDR
node1   10.42.0.0/24
node2   10.42.1.0/24
node3   10.42.2.0/24

# RKE2 defaults
#   cluster-cidr: 10.42.0.0/16   (pods)
#   service-cidr: 10.43.0.0/16   (services)
examples.note: Seeing 10.42.x for a pod and 10.43.x for a Service is the quickest way to orient yourself on any RKE2/K3s cluster.

examples.label: The MTU bug, in one command
examples.code:
# works
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- curl -s http://api:8080/health

# hangs forever on a large response = MTU mismatch
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- curl -s http://api:8080/big-payload

# confirm: ping with DF set, just under the encapsulated size
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- ping -M do -s 1422 10.42.2.15
examples.note: TCP handshakes and small packets pass; anything that fills a full frame is silently dropped. Check the CNI MTU against the underlay, especially on VMs with jumbo frames or an extra tunnel.

items.prompt: What does the Kubernetes network model actually require?
choices: Every pod can reach every other pod's IP directly, without NAT
Pods must be on the same L2 broadcast domain
All pod traffic must be encrypted
Every pod must have a routable address on the physical network
items.explain: That single requirement is the whole contract; how it is met (VXLAN, BGP, cloud routes, eBPF) is the CNI's business. Everything above — Services, DNS, NetworkPolicy — assumes flat reachability.

items.prompt: What is RKE2's default CNI, and what are its two halves?
choices: Canal — Flannel for the dataplane, Calico for NetworkPolicy
Cilium — eBPF for both dataplane and policy
Calico alone, in BGP mode
kubenet with cloud routes
items.explain: Canal is the Flannel+Calico combination: VXLAN overlay from Flannel, policy enforcement from Calico. RKE2 also supports Calico, Cilium and Multus, chosen via `cni:` in `/etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml` — at cluster creation time, not afterwards.

items.prompt: Small HTTP requests between pods on different nodes succeed; large responses hang and time out. Most likely cause?
choices: MTU mismatch — VXLAN overhead is not accounted for, so full-size frames are dropped
A NetworkPolicy blocking the response
CoreDNS returning stale records
kube-proxy iptables rules out of order
items.explain: Classic signature: the handshake and small payloads fit, big ones do not. Policies block connections outright, DNS fails at resolution. Check the CNI MTU against the underlay, minus ~50 bytes for VXLAN.

items.prompt: Two containers in the same pod both try to listen on port 8080. What happens?
choices: The second fails to bind — containers in a pod share one network namespace
Both work; each container has its own network namespace
The kubelet remaps the second one to a free port
The pod is rejected at admission
items.explain: One IP and one port space per pod. That shared namespace is exactly what makes sidecars work (`localhost` calls, no service discovery) and what makes port collisions possible.

concepts.title: Services and kube-proxy
concepts.brief:
A ClusterIP is a **virtual IP that nothing listens on**. There is no process bound to `10.43.0.15`. Packets to it are rewritten in the kernel by rules that kube-proxy programs on every node.

The chain of objects:

- **Service** — defines the virtual IP, ports and a pod selector
- **EndpointSlice** — the actual backend pod IPs, maintained by the endpointslice controller from *ready* pods
- **kube-proxy** — watches both and writes iptables (default) or IPVS rules that DNAT the ClusterIP to one of the endpoints

Consequences worth internalising:

- Load balancing is per-connection and random — no least-connections, no retries, no session tracking beyond conntrack
- A pod failing its readiness probe is removed from EndpointSlices, which is what makes readiness meaningful
- A Service with **no ready endpoints** gives connection refused/timeout — `kubectl get endpointslices` is the fastest diagnosis
- **Headless** (`clusterIP: None`) skips all of this: DNS returns the pod IPs directly. That is what StatefulSets use.

examples.label: Service, EndpointSlice, iptables
examples.code:
$ kubectl get svc api
NAME   TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     PORT(S)    AGE
api    ClusterIP   10.43.12.201   80/TCP     14d

$ kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
NAME        ADDRESSTYPE   ENDPOINTS                     PORTS
api-x7k2p   IPv4          10.42.1.7,10.42.2.3           8080

$ iptables-save -t nat | grep 10.43.12.201
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.43.12.201/32 -p tcp --dport 80 -j KUBE-SVC-XN3...
-A KUBE-SVC-XN3... -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.5 -j KUBE-SEP-A...
-A KUBE-SVC-XN3... -j KUBE-SEP-B...
examples.note: That `--probability 0.5` is the entire load balancing algorithm: random per new connection.

examples.label: The empty-endpoints diagnosis
examples.code:
$ kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
NAME        ADDRESSTYPE   ENDPOINTS   PORTS
api-x7k2p   IPv4          <unset>     <unset>

# so: selector mismatch, or no pod is Ready
$ kubectl get pods -l app=api -o wide
$ kubectl get svc api -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
examples.note: Two causes, both quick to check: the selector does not match any pod's labels, or the pods exist but fail readiness.

examples.label: Service types, stacked
examples.code:
ClusterIP     virtual IP, in-cluster only              (the base)
NodePort      ClusterIP + a port on every node         (30000-32767)
LoadBalancer  NodePort + an external LB provisioned     (cloud, or MetalLB / RKE2 ServiceLB on bare metal)
ExternalName  a CNAME in DNS, no proxying at all
Headless      clusterIP: None - DNS returns pod IPs, no virtual IP

choices: A virtual IP with no listener — iptables/IPVS rules on each node DNAT it to a pod IP
An IP assigned to a proxy pod that forwards traffic
An alias on the primary interface of every node
A DNS name resolved to a random pod IP at query time
items.explain: Nothing answers ARP for it and no process binds it. This explains why you cannot ping a ClusterIP on many setups, and why tcpdump on a node shows the pod IP, not the service IP.

items.prompt: `curl api:80` from a pod gives connection refused. `kubectl get endpointslices` shows no addresses for the Service. What are the two things to check?
choices: The Service selector versus the pod labels, and whether the pods are passing readiness
CoreDNS configuration and the search domains
The NodePort range and the firewall
kube-proxy mode and conntrack table size
items.explain: EndpointSlices only ever contain *ready* pods matching the selector. Empty means either nothing matched or nothing is ready. Both are one command away, and neither is a networking problem.

items.prompt: Order what happens when a pod connects to `api:80` (a ClusterIP Service).
steps: CoreDNS resolves api.default.svc.cluster.local to the ClusterIP 10.43.12.201
The packet leaves the pod addressed to the ClusterIP
iptables/IPVS rules on the node DNAT the destination to one endpoint pod IP
The CNI routes the packet to the node hosting that pod
The reply is un-NATed by conntrack on the way back
items.explain: DNS gives you a virtual IP; the kernel gives you a real one. Knowing where each step happens tells you where to tcpdump when it breaks.

items.prompt: Why do StatefulSets use a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`)?
choices: So DNS returns individual pod IPs, giving each replica a stable, addressable name
Because StatefulSet pods cannot be load balanced
To avoid consuming an IP from the service CIDR
Because kube-proxy does not support StatefulSets
items.explain: `web-0.web.default.svc.cluster.local` resolves to that specific pod. Databases and quorum systems need to address peers individually — a random-per-connection virtual IP is useless for that.

items.prompt: You create a `type: LoadBalancer` Service on a bare-metal RKE2 cluster with no cloud provider and no MetalLB. What happens?
choices: RKE2's built-in ServiceLB (klipper-lb) can claim it using node IPs — otherwise it stays Pending with no external IP
It automatically falls back to NodePort behaviour with an external IP
The API server rejects the Service
kube-proxy assigns an IP from the service CIDR
items.explain: Nothing in core Kubernetes implements LoadBalancer — a controller must. RKE2 ships ServiceLB (enabled unless you set `disable-kube-proxy`/`disable: rke2-servicelb`), which runs a DaemonSet claiming the port on node IPs. MetalLB is the usual alternative for a real VIP.

concepts.title: CoreDNS and resolution
concepts.brief:
CoreDNS runs as a Deployment; its Service (`kube-dns` in `kube-system`, usually `10.43.0.10`) is written into every pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` by the kubelet.

The part that surprises people is `ndots:5`. Any name with fewer than 5 dots is tried against every search domain **first** (see the resolv.conf below).

So `api.github.com` (2 dots) becomes four queries: `api.github.com.prod.svc.cluster.local`, `...svc.cluster.local`, `...cluster.local`, and finally `api.github.com`. Three NXDOMAINs before the answer. At high request rates this is a real source of latency and of CoreDNS load — the reason `dnsConfig` overrides and trailing-dot FQDNs exist.

Service names resolve as `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. Same namespace: `api` works. Different namespace: you need `api.other`.

examples.label: What a pod's resolver looks like
examples.code:
$ kubectl exec -it debug -n prod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.43.0.10
search prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5

$ kubectl exec -it debug -n prod -- nslookup api
Name:   api.prod.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.43.12.201

examples.label: Cutting the search-domain tax
examples.code:
spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
    - name: ndots
      value: "2"
# or use a fully qualified name with a trailing dot in the app:
#   https://api.github.com.
examples.note: For a service making many external calls, this removes three failed lookups per request.

examples.label: Is it DNS, or is it the Service?
examples.code:
# resolves but nothing answers -> Service/endpoints problem
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- nslookup api.prod
$ kubectl exec -it debug -- nc -zv 10.43.12.201 80

# does not resolve at all -> CoreDNS or resolv.conf problem
$ kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50
$ kubectl -n kube-system get cm rke2-coredns-rke2-coredns -o yaml

items.prompt: A pod in namespace `prod` calls `api.github.com`. With default `ndots:5`, how many DNS queries are made?
choices: Four — three search-domain attempts that NXDOMAIN, then the name itself
One — it is already a fully qualified name
Two — cluster.local then the real name
Eight — each search domain tried for A and AAAA
items.explain: Fewer than 5 dots means the search list is tried first. Three wasted round trips per lookup, on every external call. Fix with `dnsConfig.options ndots:2` or a trailing dot to make the name absolute. (With IPv6 enabled it really is doubled — the AAAA queries too.)

items.prompt: From a pod in namespace `prod`, what is the shortest name that resolves the Service `api` in namespace `payments`?
items.explain: `api.payments` — the search domain `svc.cluster.local` completes it. A bare `api` would resolve to `api.prod.svc.cluster.local`, which is a different Service (or nothing at all).

items.prompt: `nslookup api.prod` returns the ClusterIP correctly, but connections to it time out. Where is the fault?
choices: Not DNS — look at endpoints, readiness, NetworkPolicy or the app's listen address
CoreDNS is returning a stale record
The search domains are wrong
kubelet wrote the wrong nameserver into resolv.conf
items.explain: Resolution succeeded, so DNS did its job. Next: does the Service have ready endpoints, is a NetworkPolicy dropping the connection, and is the container actually listening on 0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1?

items.prompt: CoreDNS pods are CPU-throttled and DNS latency across the cluster has spiked. Which is the *least* useful fix?
choices: Increase the Service's ClusterIP range
Scale up CoreDNS replicas / raise its CPU limit
Lower ndots for chatty workloads to cut query volume
Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache
items.explain: The service CIDR has nothing to do with DNS load. The other three all attack the real problem: more capacity, fewer queries, or a per-node cache that keeps lookups off the network entirely.

concepts.title: Ingress and NetworkPolicy
concepts.brief:
An **Ingress** object is just configuration. Without a controller reading it, nothing happens. RKE2 ships **ingress-nginx** as a DaemonSet by default, deployed through its helm-controller.

The path in: external LB / node port 80/443 → ingress controller pod → *directly to a backend pod IP* (the controller reads EndpointSlices itself and usually bypasses the ClusterIP entirely).

**NetworkPolicy** is deny-by-default *once a pod is selected by any policy*:

- A pod matched by no policy accepts everything
- A pod matched by any policy with an `ingress` section accepts only what those rules allow
- Ingress and egress are independent — an egress policy on the client and an ingress policy on the server must **both** allow the traffic
- It is enforced by the CNI. Under Canal it is Calico doing the work; a CNI without policy support silently ignores your policies

And the classic outage: a default-deny egress policy that forgets to allow UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system, which breaks DNS for every selected pod.

examples.label: Default deny, then allow what you need
examples.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}            # every pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system }
      podSelector:
        matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns }
    ports:
    - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
    - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
examples.note: Always ship the DNS allowance in the same commit as the default-deny. Forgetting it breaks everything in the namespace at once, in a way that looks like an application bug.

examples.label: Ingress, and who implements it
examples.code:
$ kubectl get ingressclass
NAME    CONTROLLER                      DEFAULT
nginx   k8s.io/ingress-nginx            true

$ kubectl -n kube-system get ds rke2-ingress-nginx-controller
NAME                            DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
rke2-ingress-nginx-controller   3         3         3
examples.note: On RKE2 it is a DaemonSet using hostPorts 80/443 — so your external load balancer points at the node IPs.

items.prompt: You apply an Ingress on a cluster with no ingress controller installed. What happens?
choices: The object is stored and does nothing — no address is ever assigned
The API server rejects it
kube-proxy programs rules for it
It behaves as a NodePort Service
items.explain: Same pattern as CRDs: the object is inert without a controller. `kubectl get ingress` showing an empty ADDRESS column forever is the tell.

items.prompt: Pod A is selected by a NetworkPolicy that allows ingress from pods labelled `role=frontend`. Pod B (`role=batch`) tries to connect. Pod C is selected by no policy at all. What is true?
choices: B is blocked from A; C still accepts traffic from everyone
B is blocked, and C is blocked too — policies are namespace-wide
B is allowed because policies only apply to egress
C is blocked because a default-deny is implied cluster-wide
items.explain: Selection is what flips a pod into deny-by-default. Unselected pods are wide open. This is why 'we have NetworkPolicies' means little without a namespace-wide default-deny.

items.prompt: After applying a default-deny egress policy in `prod`, every app reports 'connection timeout' to *external* APIs and to other services. What did you forget?
choices: To allow egress on port 53 to CoreDNS — nothing can resolve names any more
To allow ingress from the ingress controller
To label the namespace
To restart the CNI DaemonSet
items.explain: DNS is egress traffic too. Without a rule permitting UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns, every lookup times out and every dependency looks broken at once. Ship the allow-dns policy alongside the default-deny, always.

items.prompt: Namespace `a` has a default-deny egress policy. Namespace `b` allows ingress from namespace `a`. Can a pod in `a` reach a pod in `b`?
choices: No — the egress policy in `a` must also allow it; both directions are evaluated independently
Yes — an ingress allow on the destination is sufficient
Yes, if both namespaces are in the same cluster CIDR
Only if a NetworkPolicy exists in kube-system permitting it
items.explain: Egress is evaluated at the source, ingress at the destination, and both must permit the flow. Debugging policy issues means checking both ends — a habit that saves a lot of time.
